Sichel distribution

sichel.Rd

Probability mass function, distribution function and random generation for the Sichel distribution.

Usage

dsichel(x, mu, sigma, nu, log = FALSE)

psichel(q, mu, sigma, nu, lower.tail = TRUE, log.p = FALSE)

rsichel(n, mu, sigma, nu)

Arguments

x

vector of non-negative counts.

mu

mean parameter, must be positive.

sigma

dispersion parameter, must be positive.

nu

shape parameter, any real number.

log

logical; if TRUE, probabilities are returned on the log scale.

q

vector of quantiles.

lower.tail

logical; if TRUE (default), probabilities are \(P[X \le q]\), otherwise \(P[X > q]\).

log.p

logical; if TRUE, probabilities are returned on the log scale.

n

number of random values to return (for rsichel).

Value

dsichel gives the probability mass function, psichel gives the distribution function, and rsichel generates random deviates.

Details

This implementation allows for automatic differentiation with RTMB.

The Sichel distribution is a mixed Poisson distribution whose mean follows a generalised inverse Gaussian distribution. In the parameterisation of the SICHEL family of the gamlss.dist package, \(\mu\) is the mean and the probability mass function is $$P(X = x) = \frac{(\mu/c)^x\, K_{x + \nu}(\alpha)}{x!\,(\alpha\sigma)^{x + \nu} K_\nu(1/\sigma)}, \qquad \alpha^2 = \frac{1}{\sigma^2} + \frac{2\mu}{c\,\sigma}, \quad c = \frac{K_{\nu + 1}(1/\sigma)}{K_\nu(1/\sigma)},$$ for \(x = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\), where \(K_\nu\) is the modified Bessel function of the second kind. The variance is $$\mathrm{Var}(X) = \mu + \mu^2\left(\frac{2\sigma(\nu + 1)}{c} + \frac{1}{c^2} - 1\right).$$ For \(\nu = -1/2\) this is the Poisson-inverse Gaussian distribution, and as \(\sigma \to \infty\) with \(\nu > 0\) it approaches the negative binomial.

The Bessel functions are evaluated with RTMB's besselK for orders up to 50. For larger orders, besselK overflows when its argument is small, so its uniform asymptotic expansion for large orders is used instead, which is accurate to about \(10^{-10}\) on the log scale there. Both are differentiable in the order, so \(\nu\) can be estimated.

The distribution function has no closed form and is computed by summing the probability mass function over \(0, \ldots, q\), so its cost grows with the largest q. It is AD-compatible in the parameters, while q must be numeric data. This is also what one-step-ahead (OSA) residuals via RTMB::oneStepPredict need, so these are supported, e.g. with method = "cdf" and discrete = TRUE.

References

Sichel, H. S. (1982) Repeat-buying and the generalized inverse Gaussian-Poisson distribution. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society, Series C, 31, 193-204.

Rigby, R. A., Stasinopoulos, D. M., Heller, G. Z., and De Bastiani, F. (2019) Distributions for modeling location, scale, and shape: Using GAMLSS in R, Chapman and Hall/CRC, doi:10.1201/9780429298547. An older version can be found in https://www.gamlss.com/.

Olver, F. W. J. et al. (eds.) NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, equation 10.41.4, https://dlmf.nist.gov/10.41.

See also

pig, nbinom2, bnbinom2

Examples

set.seed(123)
x <- rsichel(5, mu = 4, sigma = 0.5, nu = 1)
d <- dsichel(x, mu = 4, sigma = 0.5, nu = 1)
p <- psichel(x, mu = 4, sigma = 0.5, nu = 1)
